summary: Describes the extensions to RSVP-TE signaling required to support Generalized MPLS. GMPLS extends the MPLS control plane beyond packets to time-division, wavelength and spatial switching, as in SONET, SDH and optical networks.

eli5.summary: This is the version of the GMPLS rules for another signaling system, RSVP-TE, letting it build paths over fibers and light colors as well as packet networks.

questions: how does gmpls set up bidirectional lsps
what is the rsvp notify message
subtitle: How the RSVP-TE signaling protocol is extended to set up paths across optical, time-division and fiber switches, not just packet routers.

tldr.problem: MPLS signaling with RSVP-TE was built for packet networks, but Generalized MPLS must also set up paths through time-division (SONET/SDH), wavelength (lambda) and fiber switches, which need new label formats, bidirectional paths and better failure handling.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3473 adds new RSVP objects (Generalized Label Request, Generalized Label, Label Set, Upstream Label, Admin Status, Notify Request and others), a Notify message, interface identification for separate control channels, and Hello-based restart procedures.
tldr.outcome: It is the RSVP-TE specific companion to RFC 3471. It is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, though 14 later RFCs update it.

today: RFC 3473 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 4003, RFC 4201, RFC 4420, RFC 4783, RFC 4873, RFC 4874, RFC 4974, RFC 5063, RFC 5151, RFC 5420, RFC 6002, RFC 6003, RFC 6780 and RFC 8359. Read it together with RFC 3471.

sections.title: Why GMPLS Needs RSVP-TE Extensions
sections.content:
Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extends MPLS from packet-switching interfaces (PSC) to three more classes: Time-Division Multiplex (TDM), Lambda Switch (LSC) and Fiber-Switch (FSC). The abstract names the examples: SONET/SDH time-division, optical wavelengths (lambdas), and spatial switching from an incoming port or fiber to an outgoing one.

RFC 3471 gives the generic functional description. RFC 3473 is its companion and presents the RSVP-TE specific formats and mechanisms, so its structure parallels RFC 3471. Beyond the generalization itself, it also defines RSVP-TE features for rapid failure notification. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: MPLS was built for sending little packets along pre-booked routes. GMPLS stretches the same idea to booking whole wavelengths of light and whole fibers.

sections.title: Label Formats and Label Control
sections.content:
The Generalized Label Request object (Class-Num 19, C-Type 4) rides in a Path message. It carries an LSP Encoding Type, a Switching Type and a G-PID. The ingress node sets it, transit nodes pass it on (the Switching Type may be updated hop by hop), and the egress uses it. A node that cannot support the encoding or switching type MUST send a PathErr, and an unsupported G-PID is normally caught at the egress.

The Generalized Label object (Class-Num 16, C-Type 2) travels upstream in Resv messages. Waveband switching uses C-Type 3 with a Waveband Id, a Start Label and an End Label. When a waveband is switched in a way that mirrors wavelengths about a center frequency, the start and end labels MUST be flipped before the label is forwarded.

Other label objects give an upstream node control over what downstream picks:

  • Suggested_Label (Class-Number 129) in a Path message hints at a preferred label. Errors in it MUST be ignored, and an ingress node SHOULD NOT send traffic on a suggested label until the downstream node passes a matching label upstream.
  • Label_Set (Class-Number 36) restricts the labels allowed downstream. Its Action field (0 to 3) adds or excludes specific labels or ranges. An empty intersection ends the request with a PathErr.
  • The Label ERO subobject and Label RRO subobject (both Type 3) allow explicit label control. Up to two label subobjects may be present, one for downstream and one for upstream.
sections.eli5: A label is like a lane number. These objects let a sender say what kind of lane it needs, suggest one, or give a short list of lanes that are allowed.

sections.title: Bidirectional Paths and Administrative Status
sections.content:
A bidirectional LSP is requested by including an Upstream_Label object (Class-Number 35) in the Path message. The label MUST be valid for forwarding when the Path message is sent. The terminating node can use the upstream label immediately to send data back toward the initiator. If an intermediate node cannot allocate a label or internal resources it MUST issue a PathErr. When two neighbors might set up paths at once, the node ID for contention purposes is the IP address in the RSVP_HOP object, and a node that does not know its neighbor's ID should suggest a label chosen at random.

The optional Admin_Status object (Class-Number 196) carries the administrative state of an LSP in Path and Resv messages, with a Reflect (R) bit, a Delete (D) bit and two further low-order bits, T and A. It supports a graceful delete: the ingress first sends a Path message with the R and D bits set, and only after the status is reflected back in a Resv message does it send a PathTear. If the egress does not support the object, the ingress SHOULD wait only a configurable period, 30 seconds by default, before sending PathTear.
sections.eli5: A two-way road needs lanes in both directions, so the request names the return lane too. Before closing a road, the sender announces the closure and waits for an answer, so nobody is caught driving on it.

sections.title: Notification and Faster Failure Reports
sections.content:
Ordinary RSVP errors only travel hop by hop. RFC 3473 adds three notification tools so the node responsible for restoring a failed LSP hears quickly.

  • The Notify_Request object (Class-Number 195, IPv4 or IPv6) names the node to be told about a failure. It can be placed in Path messages for upstream notification or Resv messages for downstream notification.
  • The Notify message (Message Type 21) can be sent to a non-adjacent node, either forwarded normally or encapsulated in a new IP header addressed to the target. It is sent without the router alert option and MUST NOT be generated unless a Notify Request was received. Notifications to the same node with the same ERROR_SPEC SHOULD be combined, using a default notification interval of 1 ms, and delivery SHOULD be reliable using the Ack message from RFC 2961.
  • The Path_State_Removed flag (0x04) in ERROR_SPEC lets intermediate nodes remove Path state on certain errors and generate a PathTear, so resources are freed sooner and control load is lower.

The Acceptable_Label_Set object (Class-Number 130) can be added to PathErr and ResvErr messages to tell the sender which labels would have been acceptable.
sections.eli5: Normally bad news is passed from neighbor to neighbor. Here, a station can ask to be called directly when something breaks, so the right person finds out right away.

sections.title: Control Channels, Protection and Fault Recovery
sections.content:
In optical networks the control channel may be separate from the data channel. The sender of a Path message picks the data interface and names it in a new IF_ID RSVP_HOP object (Class-Num 3, C-Type 3 for IPv4 and 4 for IPv6) using TLVs. The matching IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object (Class-Num 6) names the interface involved in an error. The optional Protection object (Class-Number 37) requests link protection attributes, and a transit node that cannot satisfy it MUST send a PathErr.

Fault handling covers two cases: control channel faults, where communication between two nodes is lost, and nodal faults, where a node loses its control state but keeps forwarding state. Both rely on the Restart_Cap object (Class-Num 131) in Hello messages. It has two 32-bit fields in milliseconds: Restart Time, and Recovery Time, where zero means forwarding state was not preserved.

A node that loses contact with a neighbor that supports recovery SHOULD wait at least the neighbor's Restart Time before acting, and should keep the state of established LSPs. For a control channel fault it refreshes shared state, ideally with Summary Refreshes, within the Recovery Time. For a nodal fault the restarting node uses the Recovery_Label object (Class-Number 34) to match Path messages to its preserved forwarding entries. Its neighbor SHOULD refresh Path state within about half the advertised Recovery Time and spread the messages out to avoid overloading the restarting node.
sections.eli5: If a control room goes dark but the trains keep running, the neighbors wait a bit instead of stopping everything. When the room comes back, they re-confirm who is on which track.

sections.title: RSVP Message Formats and Addressing
sections.content:
Section 10 summarizes how RSVP messages change. Path messages gain optional PROTECTION, LABEL_SET, NOTIFY_REQUEST and ADMIN_STATUS objects, and the sender descriptor can carry SUGGESTED_LABEL and RECOVERY_LABEL, plus a required UPSTREAM_LABEL for bidirectional LSPs. PathErr and ResvErr can carry ACCEPTABLE_LABEL_SET, Resv gains NOTIFY_REQUEST and ADMIN_STATUS, and Hello gains an optional RESTART_CAP.

Addressing also changes. Standard RSVP puts the session destination in the IP header of Path, PathTear and ResvConf, since it assumes routes can change and non-RSVP hops may exist. In generalized signaling routes are usually explicit and every hop must be able to allocate labels. So when the next hop is known to be adjacent at the data plane, a node SHOULD address these messages directly to an address of that node's control plane, without the router alert option.
sections.eli5: The message layouts just get a few new optional boxes. And since the route is already decided, messages can be mailed straight to the next station instead of to the far end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSVP message security from RFC 2747 provides message integrity and node authentication, and for hop-by-hop messages this document adds no new security considerations. The new risk is the Notify message, which can be sent in a non-hop-by-hop way and so bypasses RSVP's hop-by-hop integrity and authentication model.

Where the same protection is wanted, standard IPsec can be used in transport mode, with AH or ESP. An automated key management system, most likely IKE, SHOULD be used to permit replay detection, though configured keys MAY be used. Where IPsec is unavailable and security is required, Notify messages MUST be sent hop by hop. Alternatively, non-hop-by-hop Notify messages can be disabled.
sections.eli5: Because a Notify message can skip stations and go straight to its target, the usual hop-by-hop checks do not apply. So either lock the message with IPsec or send it station to station.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The new objects each get C-Types. Suggested_Label, Upstream_Label and Recovery_Label inherit their C-Type values from the Label object (class 16), and Acceptable_Label_Set follows Label_Set. For Label_Set, Notify_Request, Protection, Admin Status and Restart_Cap, C-Types 0x00 to 0x3F are allocated by IETF Consensus, 0x40 to 0x5F First Come First Served, and 0x60 to 0x7F are reserved for Private Use.

The Notify message is Message Type 21, and new error values were assigned under "Routing problem" and "Notify Error", listed in the table below.
sections.eli5: New message types and codes need official numbers so that everyone uses the same ones. IANA is the keeper of that list.

viz.caption: GRACEFUL LSP DELETION FROM THE INGRESS (RFC 3473 SECTION 7.2.1)

messages.label: Path with Admin_Status (R and D bits set)
messages.note: Ingress announces the deletion before tearing down.

messages.label: Resv with Admin_Status (D bit set)
messages.note: Egress reflects the values, with the R bit cleared.

messages.label: PathTear
messages.note: Normal RSVP teardown then takes place.

items.desc: No label could be chosen from the Label Set, or it could not be parsed.

items.desc: The Switching Type is not supported on the incoming interface.

items.label: Routing problem / Unsupported Encoding
items.desc: The LSP Encoding Type cannot be supported.

items.label: Routing problem / Unsupported Link Protection

items.desc: The control channel has been restored.

items.desc: Control communication with a neighbor has been lost.
